name: Thaddaeus (Judas of James)
title: One of the Twelve
tagline: Two names in the lists, and one question at the Last Supper.

family.text: Luke and Acts name him by his relation to a James. The Greek gives only the genitive, literally Judas of James; the KJV prints “the brother” as a supplied word, and the Revised Version of 1881 reads the son of James. Who this James was, Scripture does not say.

identifications.text: This page treats Thaddaeus (Matthew 10, Mark 3) and Judas of James (Luke 6, Acts 1) as one man: each stands in the third group of four (tenth in Matthew and Mark, eleventh in Luke and Acts), and no list has both names. Jerome (as McGiffert and Kerr report), McGiffert (1890) and Kerr (ISBE, 1915) hold this; Kerr calls it “generally accepted”.
John's “Judas … not Iscariot” at the Last Supper is taken to be this Judas, the only other Judas in the lists.

The texts differ at Matthew 10:3. The KJV, following the Textus Receptus, reads “Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus”; Tischendorf's Greek text (1869-72) has “Lebbaeus” alone, and the Revised Version (1881) “Thaddaeus” alone.

The last verse that names him is Acts 1:13. After that Acts speaks of “the eleven” and “the twelve” as a body (Acts 2:14; 6:2) but never names him again.

Named next to him in all four lists.

scripture.text: Scripture does not mention him after Acts 1:13 and records nothing of his death.

tradition.text: Eusebius says that after the ascension Thomas sent “Thaddeus, who was also numbered among the seventy disciples of Christ” to King Abgar at Edessa, translating the story from Syriac records he says were kept there. Eusebius counts this Thaddaeus among the Seventy, not the Twelve; McGiffert (1890) calls that an error and notes that Eusebius is the first known to tell the story.
The Greek “Acts of the Holy Apostle Thaddaeus” makes him one of the Twelve, born at Edessa; after preaching in Syria he “fell asleep” at Berytus (Beirut) and was buried there.

questions.question: Are Thaddaeus and Judas of James one man? (Most widely held view first.)

views.label: One man
views.holders: Jerome, Commentary on Matthew (late 4th century), as reported by McGiffert and Kerr; A. C. McGiffert (1890); C. M. Kerr, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Each stands in the third group of four (tenth in Matthew and Mark, eleventh in Luke and Acts), and no list has both names.

views.label: Two men
views.holders: Ewald and others, as reported by C. M. Kerr (ISBE, 1915)

argument.text: On this view Thaddaeus died during Jesus' lifetime and Judas was chosen in his place.

views.label: A Thaddaeus of the Seventy
views.holders: Eusebius, Church History 1.12.3 and 1.13 (about AD 325), reporting what “they say”

argument.text: Eusebius counts the Thaddaeus sent to Edessa among the seventy disciples, not the Twelve. McGiffert (1890) calls this an error like the one that made Cephas a different man from Peter.

questions.question: Was he the brother of James, or the son of James? (In the order the readings appeared in English.)

views.label: Brother of James
views.holders: the KJV translators (1611), who supplied “the brother”; Jacobus de Voragine (about 1260), who calls him “brother to James the Less”

argument.text: The letter of Jude opens with a Jude who is “brother of James”; read beside that verse, the supplied word “brother” fits.

views.label: Son of James
views.holders: the Revised Version (1881); C. M. Kerr, ISBE (1915): “The latter is to be preferred”

argument.text: The Greek has the same bare genitive as for James of Alphaeus in the verse before, where the KJV itself supplies “the son”.

questions.question: Is he Jude, the Lord's brother and the writer of the letter of Jude? (In the order the sources give them.)

argument.text: The writer of Jude calls himself “brother of James”, and the Lord's brothers included a James and a Judas.

views.label: No
views.holders: A. C. McGiffert (1890); C. M. Kerr, ISBE (1915); Easton himself under “Lebbaeus”

argument.text: John says the Lord's brothers did not believe in him, and if Luke means son of James, this Judas cannot be the Jude who is “brother of James”.

notSaid: Scripture records one sentence from him, his question in John 14:22, and nothing else he said or did.
Scripture does not say where he came from, what his trade was, where he went or how he died.
Scripture does not say that he wrote the letter of Jude.

story.short: Named Thaddaeus in the lists of Matthew and Mark; Luke and Acts have no Thaddaeus but list "Judas the brother of James"; Scripture says little more.

paragraphs.text: Matthew lists "Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus", and Mark lists "Thaddaeus". Luke and Acts have no Thaddaeus, but list "Judas the brother of James".

John's Gospel records one question from a disciple named "Judas ... not Iscariot": "how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world?" Jesus answered that if a man loves him he will keep his words, and that he and the Father will come to him. John does not say more of who this Judas was.

He was chosen with the Twelve and sent out with them, and he was with the Eleven in the upper room. Scripture says very little about him: no home, family or trade, and nothing after that. The letter of Jude is from "Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James"; Scripture does not say whether that Jude is this apostle.

lines.t: And he ordained twelve, that they should be with him, and that he might send them forth to preach,
of them he chose twelve, whom also he named apostles;
And Judas the brother of James,
Go not into the way of the Gentiles, and into any city of the Samaritans enter ye not:
He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them, he it is that loveth me: and he that loveth me shall be loved of my Father, and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him.
Judas saith unto him, not Iscariot,
Lord, how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world?
If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him.
